label: Birds of prey lay few eggs, the kestrel excepted
claim: All birds of prey (birds with crooked talons) are unprolific, except the kestrel, which is the most prolific of them and lays four or occasionally more eggs.
quote: All birds of prey, or birds with crooked talons, are unprolific, except the kestrel: this bird is the most prolific of birds of prey; as many as four eggs have been observed in the nest, and occasionally it lays even more.
scope: birds of prey (raptors: eagles, hawks, falcons, vultures) compared with the kestrel
measurable_quantities: annual fecundity of the common kestrel versus other raptors
candidate_data: Clutch-size compilations such as the Amniote Life-History Database and Animal Diversity Web species accounts; AVONET for taxonomic coverage.

label: Long pointed eggs hatch females, rounded eggs males
claim: In birds, long and pointed eggs produce females, while round eggs, or eggs more rounded at the narrow end, produce males.
quote: Long and pointed eggs are female; those that are round, or more rounded at the narrow end, are male.
candidate_data: Poultry-science studies relating egg shape to embryo sex by molecular sexing; avian egg-shape measurements such as those compiled by Stoddard et al. (2017, Science).

label: Hens and geese lay wind-eggs without copulation
claim: Wind-eggs are not residues of earlier matings: hens and geese lay wind-eggs without ever having copulated.
quote: Such as affirm that wind-eggs are the residua of eggs previously begotten from copulation are mistaken in this assertion, for we have cases well authenticated where chickens of the common hen and goose have laid wind-eggs without ever having been subjected to copulation.
scope: domestic hen and goose; wind-eggs (unfertilized eggs)
measurable_quantities: egg production by virgin, isolated females
fertility status of eggs laid without mating
candidate_data: Poultry production and physiology literature on laying by unmated hens and geese.

label: A second cock before the yolk changes alters the breed of the egg
claim: If a hen carrying wind-eggs or fertile eggs is trodden by another cock before the yellow has changed to the white, the wind-eggs become fertile and the fertile eggs take on the breed of the second cock.
quote: Wind-eggs can turn into fertile eggs, and eggs due to previous copulation can change breed, if before the change of the yellow to the white the hen that contains wind-eggs, or eggs begotten of copulation be trodden by another cock-bird.
scope: domestic hen and other birds that lay wind-eggs
measurable_quantities: paternity of chicks after sequential matings with different males
timing of mating relative to egg formation
candidate_data: Poultry sperm-competition and paternity studies using breed markers or molecular parentage.

label: Hen eggs hatch in eighteen days in summer, up to twenty-five in winter
claim: Eggs under brooding hens hatch faster in summer than in winter: in eighteen days in summer, but occasionally taking as many as twenty-five in winter.
quote: Eggs are hatched under brooding hens more rapidly in summer than in winter; that is to say, hens hatch in eighteen days in summer, but occasionally in winter take as many as twenty-five.
measurable_quantities: effect of ambient temperature on incubation duration
candidate_data: Poultry incubation literature on hatching time versus incubation temperature; AnAge incubation records for Gallus gallus.

label: Incubation time varies with the size of the parent birds
claim: The time from mating to laying and from laying to hatching is not the same for all birds but varies with the size of the parent birds, being longer in larger birds.
quote: The generation of the egg after copulation and the generation of the chick from the subsequent hatching of the egg are not brought about within equal periods for all birds, but differ as to time according to the size of the parent-birds.
candidate_data: The Amniote Life-History Database and AnAge (incubation period, body mass) with AVONET for body size across bird species.

label: The heart is the first organ seen in the hen's egg, a beating blood speck
claim: In the hen's egg the first sign of the embryo appears after three days and three nights, and the heart appears first as a speck of blood in the white that beats as though alive.
quote: With the common hen after three days and three nights there is the first indication of the embryo; with larger birds the interval being longer, with smaller birds shorter. Meanwhile the yolk comes into being, rising towards the sharp end, where the primal element of the egg is situated, and where the egg gets hatched; and the heart appears, like a speck of blood, in the white of the egg.
scope: domestic hen embryo, with the timing scaled for larger and smaller birds
measurable_quantities: day of first visible heartbeat in chick embryos
candidate_data: Chick embryo staging tables (Hamburger-Hamilton stages) and descriptive embryology of the chick heart.

label: In bird and fish embryos the head, eyes and upper parts are largest at first
claim: In both birds and fishes, development takes place at the upper part of the egg, with vessels extending from the heart, and at first the head, the eyes and the upper parts are the largest; the egg substance is then absorbed into the embryo.
quote: development takes place at the upper part of the egg, and the veins extend in like manner, at first from the heart; and at first the head, the eyes, and the upper parts are largest; and as the creature grows the egg-substance decreases and eventually disappears
measurable_quantities: relative size of head and eyes versus trunk across embryonic stages
candidate_data: Embryo staging series for chicken and zebrafish (Hamburger-Hamilton; ZFIN staging), and MorphoSource embryo scans.

label: The pigeon lays one male and one female egg, the male first
claim: The pigeon, as a rule, lays one male and one female egg, generally the male egg first, with a day's interval before the second.
quote: The pigeon, as a rule, lays a male and a female egg, and generally lays the male egg first; after laying it allows a day's interval to ensue and then lays the second egg.
measurable_quantities: sex composition of two-egg pigeon clutches
sex of first- versus second-laid egg
candidate_data: Studies of sex ratio and laying order in Columba livia clutches using molecular sexing.

label: Eagle mothers expel one of their two chicks from the nest
claim: The eagle usually rears two young from three eggs, and as the young grow the mother, wearied with feeding them, ejects one of the pair from the nest.
quote: This is the case in most instances, though occasionally a brood of three has been observed. As the young ones grow, the mother becomes wearied with feeding them and extrudes one of the pair from the nest.
measurable_quantities: clutch size and fledged brood size in eagles
cause of loss of the second chick (sibling aggression versus parental ejection)
candidate_data: Raptor breeding studies on brood reduction and siblicide (e.g. in Aquila eagles); Animal Diversity Web species accounts.

label: The cuckoo lays in other birds' nests after eating their eggs
claim: The cuckoo builds no nest but lays its egg, usually one and occasionally two, in the nest of a smaller bird after first devouring that bird's eggs.
quote: The bird eggs, but does not build a nest. Sometimes it lays its eggs in the nest of a smaller bird after first devouring the eggs of this bird; it lays by preference in the nest of the ringdove, after first devouring the eggs of the pigeon. (It occasionally lays two, but usually one.)
scope: the common cuckoo and its hosts
measurable_quantities: number of cuckoo eggs per host nest
removal of host eggs at laying
candidate_data: Brood-parasitism studies of Cuculus canorus and host-record compilations; Animal Diversity Web and EltonTraits for nesting behaviour.

label: Male birds' testicles enlarge at pairing time
claim: In male birds the testicles are obviously larger at pairing time than at other times, most conspicuously in the more salacious birds such as the cock and the cock partridge.
quote: With male birds about pairing time the testicles are obviously larger than at other times, and this is conspicuously the case with the more salacious birds, such as the barn-door cock and the cock partridge
scope: male birds, especially the domestic cock and partridge
measurable_quantities: testis mass across the breeding cycle
relative testis size versus mating frequency
candidate_data: Avian testis-size and seasonal gonadal recrudescence datasets in the comparative literature.

label: Swallow chicks recover their sight after their eyes are pricked out
claim: If the eyes of young swallow chicks are pricked out, the birds recover and later see again.
quote: If you prick out the eyes of swallow chicks while they are yet young, the birds will get well again and will see by and by.
measurable_quantities: recovery of vision after eye injury in nestling birds
candidate_data: Avian eye regeneration and wound-repair literature; none known for swallows specifically.

label: Cartilaginous fishes are first oviparous internally, then viviparous
claim: Cartilaginous fishes are viviparous, producing eggs internally first and then bearing live young reared inside the body, the fishing-frog being an exception; all other fishes are oviparous.
quote: Fishes of the cartilaginous genus are viviparous; the rest are oviparous. And cartilaginous fishes are first oviparous internally and subsequently viviparous; they rear the embryos internally, the batrachus or fishing-frog being an exception.
scope: selachians (cartilaginous fishes: sharks and rays) versus other fishes; the fishing-frog (anglerfish)
measurable_quantities: reproductive mode (oviparous, aplacental or placental viviparous) across chondrichthyans and teleosts
candidate_data: FishBase reproduction tables and published compilations of chondrichthyan reproductive modes; Open Tree of Life for taxon coverage.

label: Smooth dogfish embryos are attached to the womb by a navel-string
claim: In the smooth shark the young develop with a navel-string attached to the womb, so that once the egg-substance is used up the embryo is sustained as in quadrupeds.
quote: these eggs shift into each of the two horns of the womb and descend, and the young develop with the navel-string attached to the womb, so that, as the egg-substance gets used up, the embryo is sustained to all appearance just as in the case of quadrupeds.
measurable_quantities: presence of a yolk-sac placenta in Mustelus species
maternal nutrient transfer after yolk depletion
candidate_data: Chondrichthyan reproductive-biology literature on placental viviparity in Mustelus; FishBase and SeaLifeBase species accounts.

label: Different kinds of fish do not interbreed, except angel-fish and skate
claim: As a general rule no kind of fish pairs with another kind, but the angel-fish and the skate appear to pair, producing the rhinobatus, which has the front of a skate and the rear of an angel-fish.
quote: Observations would lead to the general rule that no one variety of fish pairs with another variety. The angel-fish, however, and the batus or skate appear to pair with one another; for there is a fish called the rhinobatus, with the head and front parts of the skate and the after parts of the rhine or angel-fish
scope: fishes; the angel shark (Squatina), skates and the guitarfish (Rhinobatos)
measurable_quantities: frequency of natural interspecific hybridization in fishes
hybrid versus independent-lineage status of guitarfishes
candidate_data: Fish hybridization reviews; Open Tree of Life and molecular phylogenies of Batoidea and Squatiniformes.

label: Cetaceans, which have a blow-hole, are viviparous
claim: The dolphin, the whale and all other cetaceans, which have a blow-hole instead of gills, are viviparous, carrying an embryo rather than eggs, as in humans and viviparous quadrupeds.
quote: The dolphin, the whale, and all the rest of the Cetacea, all, that is to say, that are provided with a blow-hole instead of gills, are viviparous.
candidate_data: PanTHERIA and AnAge life-history records for Cetacea; Animal Diversity Web.

label: Dolphins live twenty-five to thirty years, shown by tail-notching
claim: The dolphin lives many years, some for more than twenty-five and some for thirty, as shown by fishermen who notch dolphins' tails and release them.
quote: It lives for many years; some are known to have lived for more than twenty-five, and some for thirty years; the fact is fishermen nick their tails sometimes and set them adrift again, and by this expedient their ages are ascertained.
measurable_quantities: maximum and typical lifespan of dolphins
candidate_data: AnAge maximum longevity records for Delphinus and Tursiops; long-term photo-identification studies of dolphin populations.

label: Erythrinus and channa are always caught full of eggs
claim: Unlike most fishes, which are divided into males and females, specimens of the erythrinus and the channa are never caught except in a condition of pregnancy.
quote: Fishes for the most part are divided into males and females, but one is puzzled to account for the erythrinus and the channa, for specimens of these species are never caught except in a condition of pregnancy.
scope: the erythrinus and the channa (probably sea perches of the genus Serranus) versus most fishes
measurable_quantities: presence of males in the population (hermaphroditism)
candidate_data: FishBase reproduction records for Serranus species and the literature on simultaneous hermaphroditism in serranids.

label: Only fish eggs sprinkled with milt develop
claim: Of the eggs a female fish deposits, only those over which the male sheds his milt produce young; the rest are unproductive.
quote: The greater number of these eggs so deposited are not productive, but only those over which the male sheds the milt or sperm; for when the female has laid her eggs, the male follows and sheds its sperm over them, and from all the eggs so besprinkled young fishes proceed, while the rest are left to their fate.
scope: oviparous fishes that spawn externally, and the cuttlefish
measurable_quantities: fertilization rate of eggs with and without milt exposure
candidate_data: Fish external fertilization and aquaculture fertilization-rate literature.

label: Fish spawn inshore for warmth, food and protection
claim: Fish in general deposit their eggs close to shore because the inshore water is warmer, better supplied with food, and protects the spawn from larger fish.
quote: Fish in general so deposit their eggs; for the water close in to shore is warm and is better supplied with food than the outer sea, and serves as a protection to the spawn against the voracity of the larger fish.
measurable_quantities: proportion of species spawning in nearshore versus offshore habitats
temperature, food and predation levels at spawning sites
candidate_data: FishBase spawning-habitat fields and GBIF/OBIS occurrence records of eggs and larvae.

label: The pipefish releases its eggs through a split that then heals
claim: The pipefish has a cleft growth under the belly that splits open to release its eggs at spawning, after which the sides of the split grow together again.
quote: For the fish has a diaphysis or cloven growth under the belly and abdomen (like the blind snakes), and, after it has spawned by the splitting of this diaphysis, the sides of the split grow together again.
measurable_quantities: structure and opening of the ventral brood pouch
candidate_data: Syngnathid reproductive-anatomy literature; FishBase species accounts for Syngnathus.

label: The male sheat-fish guards the spawn for forty to fifty days
claim: Because growth from the egg is exceptionally slow in the sheat-fish, the male guards the spawn for forty or fifty days to keep small fishes from eating it.
quote: In the case of the sheat-fish the growth from the egg is exceptionally slow, and, in consequence, the male has to keep watch for forty or fifty days to prevent the-spawn being devoured by such little fishes as chance to come by.
scope: the glanis or sheat-fish (probably Aristotle's catfish, Silurus aristotelis)
candidate_data: FishBase reproduction records for Silurus aristotelis and field studies of its paternal care.

label: Eels are generated spontaneously from 'earth's guts' in mud
claim: Eels do not come from pairing or from eggs; they arise from the so-called 'earth's guts', worm-like growths that form spontaneously in mud and humid ground.
quote: But this opinion is not founded on fact. Eels are derived from the so-called 'earth's guts' that grow spontaneously in mud and in humid ground; in fact, eels have at times been seen to emerge out of such earthworms
measurable_quantities: presence of gonads and gametes in eels
origin of juvenile eels (larvae, glass eels)
candidate_data: European eel life-cycle and spawning-migration studies; FishBase account of Anguilla anguilla.

label: Eels go down to the sea while mullet go up into rivers
claim: The mullet goes up from the sea into marshes and rivers, whereas eels make their way down from marshes and rivers to the sea.
quote: The mullet goes up from the sea to marshes and rivers; the eels, on the contrary, make their way down from the marshes and rivers to the sea.
measurable_quantities: direction and timing of migration between fresh water and sea
candidate_data: FishBase migration fields (catadromous, amphidromous) for Anguilla and Mugilidae; telemetry studies of eel migration.

label: Some fishes arise spontaneously from mud and sand
claim: Certain fishes come into existence spontaneously from mud or sand and decaying matter, not from eggs or copulation.
quote: From the facts above enumerated it is quite proved that certain fishes come spontaneously into existence, not being derived from eggs or from copulation.
scope: a kind of small mullet in ponds near Cnidos, the 'froth' fry, small fry in Asia Minor rivers
measurable_quantities: origin of fish appearing in refilled ponds (eggs, dormant stages, immigration)
candidate_data: Studies of fish recolonisation of temporary waters and annual killifish egg diapause.

label: Fish gestation periods are a number of days divisible by seven
claim: In all fishes the period of gestation extends over a number of days divisible by seven, never more than thirty days in some and less in others.
quote: With some fishes the time of gestation is not longer than thirty days, with others it is a lesser period; but with all it extends over a number of days divisible by seven.
measurable_quantities: duration in days of egg development or gestation across fish species
candidate_data: FishBase reproduction and egg-development records; published embryonic-duration compilations for teleosts.

label: Cartilaginous fishes are less prolific because viviparous
claim: Cartilaginous fishes are as a rule less prolific than other fishes because they are viviparous, and their young, being larger, have a better chance of escaping destruction.
quote: As a rule, cartilaginous fish are less prolific than other fish owing to their being viviparous; and their young by reason of their size have a better chance of escaping destruction.
candidate_data: FishBase fecundity and length-at-birth fields; chondrichthyan life-history compilations.

label: Males are fiercest at pairing time, females just after giving birth
claim: In animals the female is most bad-tempered just after giving birth and the male during the pairing season.
quote: The female is most cross-tempered just after parturition, the male during the time of pairing
scope: animals in general; examples include stallions, boars, bulls, rams, camels, bears, wolves, lions
measurable_quantities: rates of aggression by males in the mating season versus other seasons
candidate_data: Behavioural ecology literature on seasonal male aggression and maternal aggression in mammals.

label: Breeding seasons are timed so the young are reared at a convenient season
claim: Sexual appetite in animals is generally keenest in spring, but the pairing season differs among animals and is adapted to ensure that the young are reared at a convenient season.
quote: In general the sexual appetites of animals are keenest in spring-time; the time of pairing, however, is not the same for all, but is adapted so as to ensure the rearing of the young at a convenient season.
candidate_data: PanTHERIA and AnAge gestation lengths combined with breeding-season records from Animal Diversity Web.

label: Sheep and goats carry their young five months
claim: The ewe usually bears two lambs, sometimes three or four; ewe and she-goat both carry their young for five months, and the goat lives eight years and the sheep ten.
quote: The ewe bears usually two lambs, sometimes three or four. Both ewe and she-goat carry their young for five months; consequently wherever a district is sunny and the animals are used to comfort and well fed, they bear twice in the year. The goat lives for eight years and the sheep for ten
candidate_data: AnAge records for Ovis aries and Capra hircus; livestock reproduction literature.

label: North winds at mating give male lambs, south winds female
claim: Ewes and she-goats mated while north winds are blowing tend to bear males, and those mated while south winds are blowing tend to bear females.
quote: And if they submit to the male when north winds are blowing, they are apt to bear males; if when south winds are blowing, females.
measurable_quantities: wind direction on the day of mating
candidate_data: Flock breeding records with mating dates combined with meteorological archives; none known as a ready-made dataset.

label: Dogs shed only their canine teeth, at four months
claim: The dog sheds no teeth except the canines, which both sexes shed at four months old.
quote: The dog sheds no teeth except the so-called 'canines'; these a dog of either sex sheds when four months old.
candidate_data: Veterinary dental-development references for Canis familiaris.

label: Males are shorter-lived than females because of sexual service
claim: The male horse is shorter-lived than the female because of the sexual service it renders, and horses kept in a private stable live longer than those reared in troops.
quote: The male is less long-lived than the female by reason of the sexual service he is called on to render; and horses that are reared in a private stable live longer than such as are reared in troops.
scope: horses; the same sex difference is stated for Laconian hounds and asses
candidate_data: Equine longevity and studbook records; AnAge and comparative studies of sex differences in mammalian lifespan.

label: Hybrid foals resemble the mother more than the sire
claim: In crosses between horse and ass, the foal is more apt to resemble the mother than the sire in size, looks and vigour.
quote: In regard to size, looks, and vigour, the foal is more apt to resemble the mother than the sire.
measurable_quantities: body size and conformation of mules versus hinnies relative to each parent species
candidate_data: Equine hybrid morphometric studies comparing mules and hinnies.

label: The newborn bear cub is the smallest of all relative to its mother
claim: Of all animals the newborn bear cub is the smallest in proportion to the size of its mother, larger than a mouse but smaller than a weasel.
quote: Of all animals the newly born cub of the she bear is the smallest in proportion to the size of the mother; that is to say, it is larger than a mouse but smaller than a weasel.
measurable_quantities: neonatal mass relative to maternal mass across species
candidate_data: PanTHERIA and the Amniote Life-History Database (birth or hatching mass, adult mass).

label: Hyenas are not hermaphrodites
claim: It is untrue that every hyena has both male and female organs; the male has a male organ and a structure under the tail resembling the female organ but without a passage, and the female has the true female organ.
quote: What is recounted concerning its genital organs, to the effect that every hyena is furnished with the organ both of the male and the female, is untrue.
scope: the hyena (probably the striped hyena, Hyaena hyaena)
measurable_quantities: external genital anatomy of male and female hyenas
candidate_data: Comparative anatomy of hyaenid genitalia in the mammalogy literature; Animal Diversity Web species accounts.

label: Hares breed all year and superfoetate
claim: Hares breed and bear at all seasons, conceive again while already pregnant, and bear young every month.
quote: They breed and bear at all seasons, superfoetate during pregnancy, and bear young every month.
candidate_data: Reproductive studies of Lepus europaeus documenting superfetation; AnAge and PanTHERIA litters-per-year fields.

label: Short gestation and fast growth imply a short life in deer
claim: The brevity of the deer's gestation and the rapid growth of the fawn argue against attributing extreme longevity to it.
quote: the brevity of the period of gestation and the rapidity of growth in the fawn would not lead one to attribute extreme longevity to this creature.
scope: deer, and by implication mammals generally
candidate_data: AnAge and PanTHERIA (gestation length, growth, maximum longevity) across mammals.

label: Field-mouse plagues are not checked by predators but end after heavy rain
claim: Foxes and wild ferrets cannot keep down field mice when they are superabundant; only rain thins them, and after heavy rains they disappear rapidly.
quote: Foxes also hunt them, and the wild ferrets in particular destroy them, but they make no way against the prolific qualities of the animal and the rapidity of its breeding. When they are super-abundant, nothing succeeds in thinning them down except the rain; but after heavy rains they disappear rapidly.
scope: field mice and voles in farmland
candidate_data: Long-term vole and mouse population time series (e.g. in the Global Population Dynamics Database) with weather records.
